# How to use this subject

Applied Physiology (PHYS110) is a first-semester B.Sc Nursing course of 3 credits (60 hours of theory) under the Indian Nursing Council (INC) Regulations 2020. It explains how each body system works, how the systems keep the internal environment steady, and what changes in disease — the base for every nursing assessment you will do. Study it alongside Applied Anatomy: learn the structure there, then the function here.

## How the notes are arranged

The INC syllabus has 11 units. Some are small, so related units are joined:

| Notes file | INC unit(s) | Hours |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit 1 General physiology | I | 4 |
| Unit 2 Respiratory system | II | 6 |
| Unit 3 Digestive system | III | 8 |
| Unit 4 Circulatory system and blood | IV (circulatory) + V (blood) | 6 + 5 |
| Unit 5 Endocrine system and sensory organs | VI (endocrine) + VII (sensory organs) | 5 + 4 |
| Unit 6 Musculoskeletal system | VIII | 6 |
| Unit 7 Renal and reproductive systems | IX (renal) + X (reproductive) | 4 + 4 |
| Unit 8 Nervous system | XI | 8 |

Every notes file ends with an "Application and implication in nursing" section, because the INC lists it in every unit and examiners like to see it in essays, and a short "Remember" list for quick revision.

**Suggested routine**: read one notes file a day; draw the flow diagrams (feedback loop, cardiac conduction, clotting cascade, CSF circulation, reflex arc) from memory; learn the normal values in the tables; then write out two or three questions from the bank without looking, and check against the model answer.

## Exam pattern

Applied Anatomy and Applied Physiology are examined together in **one university theory paper of 75 marks and 3 hours**. **Section A is Applied Anatomy (37 marks)** and **Section B is Applied Physiology (38 marks)**. Internal assessment carries 25 marks, so the course total is 100.

**Section B — Applied Physiology (38 marks)** as given in INC Appendix 3:

| Part | Questions | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| MCQ | 7 × 1 | 7 |
| Essay | 1 × 10 | 10 |
| Short answer | 3 × 5 | 15 |
| Very short answer | 3 × 2 | 6 |
| **Total** | | **38** |

There is **no internal choice** in the INC pattern — every question must be answered. Plan about 90 minutes of the 3 hours for this section. Universities sometimes add their own instructions (for example separate answer books for the two sections), so confirm the exact paper format with your university.

The mock tests in this subject follow this pattern:

- **Section B paper (38 marks, 90 minutes)** — exactly the physiology half of the combined paper.
- **Quick MCQ test (20 questions, 20 minutes)** — for daily practice.

## How probability ratings work

Each question in the bank is rated **high**, **medium** or **low**:

- **High** — topics with many teaching hours and that appear often in nursing physiology papers (for example cardiac cycle, regulation of blood pressure, clotting mechanism, erythropoiesis, gastric juice, transport of oxygen, menstrual cycle, mechanism of muscle contraction, CSF, reflex arc, pain).
- **Medium** — asked every few years or as part of a larger question.
- **Low** — less common, but useful for MCQs and very short answers.

The ratings are estimates based on the weight of each unit in the syllabus and common patterns in nursing examinations. They are not a promise of what will be asked, so do not skip any unit — with no internal choice, every unit can appear.

## Where the marks usually come from

| Unit | Likely essay or short-answer topics |
| --- | --- |
| 1 General physiology | Transport across the cell membrane; body fluid compartments; homeostasis and feedback; wound healing |
| 2 Respiratory | Mechanism of breathing; lung volumes and capacities; transport of O2 and CO2; regulation of respiration; hypoxia and cyanosis |
| 3 Digestive | Gastric juice and its regulation; pancreatic juice; bile; functions of the liver; digestion and absorption of carbohydrates, proteins and fats; deglutition |
| 4 Circulatory and blood | Cardiac cycle; conduction system; cardiac output; blood pressure and its regulation; coronary circulation; erythropoiesis; clotting mechanism; blood groups; immunity |
| 5 Endocrine and sensory | Hormones of the pituitary, thyroid, adrenal; insulin; parathyroid and calcium; temperature regulation; accommodation; errors of refraction; mechanism of hearing |
| 6 Musculoskeletal | Mechanism of skeletal muscle contraction; properties of muscle; bone healing; types of joints |
| 7 Renal and reproductive | Formation of urine; GFR; micturition reflex; menstrual cycle; spermatogenesis; oogenesis; fertilisation and implantation; lactation |
| 8 Nervous system | Nerve impulse; synapse; functions of cerebellum and hypothalamus; ANS; pain and referred pain; reflex arc; CSF and blood–brain barrier; UMN vs LMN lesions |

## Scoring tips for this subject

1. **Start with a definition** and, where possible, a normal value (for example "Cardiac output is the volume of blood pumped by each ventricle per minute — about 5 L/min").
2. **Draw a labelled diagram or flow chart** in every essay: the cardiac cycle phases, conduction system, clotting cascade, oxygen dissociation curve, nephron with filtration forces, CSF pathway, reflex arc, hormonal changes in the menstrual cycle. Flow charts with arrows score well and save time.
3. **Learn the numbers** in the tables (TV 500 mL, CO 5 L/min, GFR 125 mL/min, RBC life 120 days, platelets 1.5–4 lakh/µL, CSF 150 mL). MCQs and very short answers test them often. Write "about" — exact values differ between textbooks and laboratories.
4. **Structure essays** with headings: definition → mechanism/steps → regulation → factors → disorders/alterations → nursing implications.
5. **End every essay with nursing implications** — two or three points linking the physiology to patient care.
6. **Very short answers (2 marks)**: two clear points or a definition plus one example. Do not write a page.
7. **Use the right words**: "depolarisation", "negative feedback", "autoregulation", "Frank–Starling law", "Bohr effect" — examiners look for them.
8. **Manage time**: about 20 minutes for the essay, 10 minutes per short answer, 3–4 minutes per very short answer and a few minutes for the MCQs, leaving time to check.

## Other useful notes

- Keep a separate page of normal values and revise it weekly.
- Compare pairs that are commonly confused: rods vs cones, sympathetic vs parasympathetic, UMN vs LMN, intrinsic vs extrinsic clotting, active vs passive immunity, myopia vs hypermetropia, oogenesis vs spermatogenesis.
- The last-night revision sheet collects the key facts of all eight files on one page.

# Last-night revision sheet — Applied Physiology

Values are approximate adult figures; laboratories and textbooks differ slightly — write "about".

## 1. General physiology

- Homeostasis = constant internal environment; mostly **negative feedback**; positive feedback: labour (oxytocin), clotting, LH surge.
- Transport: passive (diffusion, facilitated diffusion, osmosis, filtration) vs active (Na+–K+ pump: **3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in per ATP**; cotransport with Na+) vs vesicular (endo-/exocytosis).
- Total body water **60%** of weight: ICF 40%, ECF 20% (interstitial 15%, plasma 5%). Na+ main ECF cation (135–145 mmol/L); K+ main ICF cation (plasma 3.5–5).
- Isotonic 0.9% NaCl; hypotonic → cells swell; hypertonic → cells shrink.
- Cell cycle G1 → S → G2 → M; G0 = neurons, cardiac muscle.
- Wound healing: haemostasis → inflammation → proliferation → remodelling.

## 2. Respiratory

- Diaphragm ≈ 75% of quiet inspiration; expiration passive; intrapleural pressure −2.5 to −6 mmHg.
- Surfactant (type II cells) lowers surface tension; lack → respiratory distress syndrome in preterm babies.
- TV 500, IRV 3000, ERV 1100, RV 1200, VC 4600, TLC 5800 mL; dead space 150 mL; minute ventilation 6 L/min.
- Alveolar PO2 104 / PCO2 40; venous 40 / 45; arterial PO2 95–100.
- O2: 97% as oxyHb (1.34 mL/g Hb); CO2: 70% HCO3−, 23% carbamino, 7% dissolved; chloride shift.
- Right shift: ↑CO2, ↑H+, ↑temperature, ↑2,3-BPG (Bohr effect). CO binds Hb ~200× more than O2.
- Central chemoreceptors → H+ from CO2 (strongest drive); carotid/aortic bodies → low PO2.
- Cyanosis > 5 g/dL reduced Hb; hypoxia types: hypoxic, anaemic, stagnant, histotoxic.
- Cheyne–Stokes (waxing–waning + apnoea); Biot's (groups of breaths + apnoea).

## 3. Digestive

- Saliva 1–1.5 L/day, ptyalin; purely nervous control (VII, IX).
- Gastric juice pH 1–3.5; parietal → HCl + intrinsic factor; chief → pepsinogen; G cells → gastrin; phases cephalic 30 / gastric 60 / intestinal 10%.
- HCl: carbonic anhydrase + H+–K+ ATPase; alkaline tide.
- Pancreatic juice pH ~8; secretin → bicarbonate; CCK → enzymes + gall bladder; enterokinase → trypsin.
- Bile salts emulsify fat, form micelles; 90–95% recycled (enterohepatic). Vitamin K, A, D, E need bile.
- Glucose/galactose with Na+ (SGLT1); fats → chylomicrons → lacteals; B12 + intrinsic factor → terminal ileum.
- Movements: peristalsis (propels), segmentation (mixes), mass movements (gastrocolic reflex); defaecation centre S2–S4.

## 4. Circulation and blood

- SA node 70–80/min → AV node (0.1 s delay) → His → bundle branches → Purkinje. Heart cannot be tetanised.
- Cardiac cycle 0.8 s (systole 0.3, diastole 0.5); S1 = AV valves close; S2 = semilunar valves close.
- SV 70 mL, EF 55–70%, **CO = SV × HR ≈ 5 L/min**; Frank–Starling law.
- **BP = CO × peripheral resistance**; 120/80; pulse pressure 40; MAP ≈ DP + ⅓PP ≈ 93.
- Baroreceptors (carotid sinus IX, aortic arch X) → short term; RAAS, ADH, ANP, kidney → long term.
- Pulse 60–100/min; pulse deficit in atrial fibrillation.
- Coronary flow 225–250 mL/min (4–5% CO), mainly diastole; O2 extraction ~70%.
- Pulmonary circuit low pressure (25/8), hypoxia → vasoconstriction.
- Postural hypotension: fall ≥ 20 systolic / ≥ 10 diastolic within 3 min of standing.
- Blood 5–6 L, pH 7.35–7.45, plasma 55%; albumin → oncotic pressure.
- RBC 4.5–5.5 million/µL (M); Hb 13–17 (M), 12–15 (F) g/dL; life **120 days**; erythropoietin (kidney), iron, B12, folate.
- WBC 4,000–11,000/µL: N 50–70, L 20–40, M 2–8, E 1–4, B 0–1%. Platelets 1.5–4 lakh/µL, life 7–10 days.
- Haemostasis: spasm → platelet plug (vWF, ADP, TXA2) → coagulation → retraction → fibrinolysis (plasmin).
- Intrinsic XII → XI → IX (+VIII); extrinsic III + VII; common X → prothrombin activator → thrombin → fibrin; XIII stabilises. Vitamin K: **II, VII, IX, X**. Haemophilia A = VIII.
- BT 1–5 min; CT 4–10 min; PT ~11–16 s (INR); aPTT ~25–40 s.
- ABO: O universal donor, AB universal recipient; Rh− mother + Rh+ baby → haemolytic disease of newborn.
- IgG crosses placenta; IgA in milk/secretions; IgM first; IgE allergy. B cells → antibodies; T cells (thymus) → cell-mediated.

## 5. Endocrine and senses

- Anterior pituitary: GH, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH, prolactin. Posterior: ADH, oxytocin (made in hypothalamus).
- GH excess: gigantism / acromegaly; ADH lack: diabetes insipidus.
- T3/T4: ↑ BMR, brain growth → cretinism if lacking; iodine lack → goitre; calcitonin ↓ Ca.
- PTH ↑ Ca (bone, kidney, vitamin D); low Ca → tetany, Chvostek, Trousseau. Serum Ca 9–10.5 mg/dL.
- Insulin (β) lowers glucose; glucagon (α), adrenaline, cortisol, GH raise it. Renal threshold 180 mg/dL.
- Adrenal cortex: aldosterone (salt), cortisol (sugar, stress), androgens; medulla: adrenaline (fight or flight).
- Pineal → melatonin (circadian); thymus → T cells.
- Temperature control: hypothalamus; heat → vasodilation, sweating; cold → vasoconstriction, shivering.
- Accommodation: ciliary muscle contracts, lens more convex, pupil constricts, convergence.
- Rods: dim light, rhodopsin, vitamin A; cones: colour, fovea. Visual cortex area 17.
- Myopia → concave; hypermetropia/presbyopia → convex; astigmatism → cylindrical.
- Hearing: eardrum → ossicles → oval window → cochlea → organ of Corti → VIII → temporal lobe (41, 42); 20–20,000 Hz.
- Taste: VII (ant. 2/3), IX (post. 1/3); smell → limbic system, no thalamic relay.

## 6. Musculoskeletal

- Osteoblasts build, osteoclasts resorb; vitamin D, PTH, calcitonin, GH, sex hormones.
- Fracture healing: haematoma → inflammation → soft callus → hard callus → remodelling.
- Synovial joints: hinge, pivot, ball and socket, condyloid, saddle, plane.
- OA = cartilage wear; RA = autoimmune synovitis; gout = urate crystals.
- Contraction: ACh → AP → T tubules → Ca2+ from SR → troponin → cross-bridges (ATP) → sliding filaments; ATP needed to detach → rigor mortis.
- Cardiac: intercalated discs, syncytium, long refractory period. Smooth: calmodulin, slow sustained tone.

## 7. Renal and reproductive

- Renal blood flow 1200–1300 mL/min (20–25% CO); **GFR 125 mL/min = 180 L/day**; urine 1–1.5 L/day.
- NFP = 60 − (18 + 32) = 10 mmHg; autoregulation 80–180 mmHg (myogenic, tubuloglomerular feedback).
- PCT reabsorbs 65% Na+/water, all glucose; loop = countercurrent; ADH → water; aldosterone → Na+ in, K+ out.
- Urine: pH ~6, SG 1.010–1.025, no glucose/protein. Oliguria < 400 mL/day.
- Micturition: stretch at 300–400 mL → pelvic nerves → S2–S4 → detrusor contracts; external sphincter voluntary (pudendal).
- Menstrual cycle 28 days: menstrual 1–5, proliferative (oestrogen), ovulation day 14 (LH surge), secretory (progesterone); luteal phase 14 days.
- Oogenesis: arrest prophase I (before birth) → secondary oocyte at ovulation, arrest metaphase II → completed at fertilisation.
- Fertilisation in ampulla; capacitation, acrosome reaction, zona reaction; father decides sex.
- Implantation day 6–7; hCG keeps corpus luteum; pregnancy test.
- Breast: prolactin = milk production; oxytocin = let-down; colostrum rich in IgA.
- Spermatogenesis 64–74 days, 2–3 °C below body temperature; FSH → Sertoli; LH → Leydig → testosterone.
- Semen: seminal vesicle 60% (fructose), prostate 30% (alkaline).

## 8. Nervous system

- RMP −70 mV; threshold −55; Na+ in (depolarisation), K+ out (repolarisation); all-or-none; saltatory conduction.
- Medulla: cardiac, vasomotor, respiratory centres; pons: pneumotaxic; cerebellum: coordination (ataxia, intention tremor).
- Areas: motor 4, Broca 44, sensory 3-1-2, auditory 41-42, visual 17, Wernicke (temporal).
- Dorsal column: fine touch, proprioception; lateral spinothalamic: pain, temperature.
- UMN: spastic, brisk reflexes, Babinski +; LMN: flaccid, areflexia, wasting.
- Spinal nerves 31 pairs (8, 12, 5, 5, 1); dorsal root sensory, ventral motor.
- Sympathetic T1–L2, NA; parasympathetic III, VII, IX, X, S2–S4, ACh.
- Hypothalamus: temperature, hunger, thirst, ADH, pituitary, ANS, emotion, circadian. Hippocampus: memory; amygdala: fear.
- Semicircular canals: rotation; utricle/saccule: position, linear acceleration.
- Pain: fast Aδ (sharp), slow C (burning); gate control; endorphins; referred: heart → left arm, diaphragm → shoulder tip, appendix → umbilicus.
- Knee jerk L2–L4, ankle S1–S2, biceps C5–C6, triceps C6–C7.
- CSF: choroid plexus, 500 mL/day, 150 mL volume; lateral → III → aqueduct → IV → subarachnoid → arachnoid villi. Protein 15–45, glucose 50–80 mg/dL.
- BBB: tight junctions + astrocytes; absent at area postrema; leaky in newborns.
- GCS 3–15 (E4 V5 M6).

## In the exam hall

Definition → diagram/flow chart → steps → regulation → normal values → alterations → nursing implications. Answer every question — there is no choice.

1. Cell membrane: lipid bilayer with proteins (fluid mosaic model); lipid-soluble substances cross easily, ions and glucose need protein channels or carriers.
2. Passive transport (no ATP, down the gradient):
   a. Simple diffusion — high to low concentration; e.g. O2 and CO2 in lungs; rate rises with gradient, area, temperature and thin membrane.
   b. Facilitated diffusion — carrier protein helps (glucose via GLUT); shows saturation.
   c. Osmosis — water moves across a selectively permeable membrane from dilute to concentrated solution; osmotic pressure.
   d. Filtration — hydrostatic pressure pushes water and small solutes (glomerulus, arterial end of capillaries).
3. Active transport (uses ATP, against the gradient):
   a. Primary — Na+–K+ ATPase pumps 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in per ATP; keeps resting potential and cell volume; also Ca2+ pump, H+–K+ pump of stomach.
   b. Secondary — uses the Na+ gradient: cotransport (Na+–glucose in gut and kidney) and countertransport (Na+–H+ exchange).
4. Vesicular transport: endocytosis — phagocytosis (bacteria by neutrophils), pinocytosis (fluid), receptor-mediated (LDL); exocytosis — release of hormones, neurotransmitters, enzymes.
5. Diagram/flow chart of the types.
6. Tonicity and nursing: isotonic (0.9% NaCl) — no change in cell size, expands ECF; hypotonic — water enters cells, cells swell (risk of brain swelling, haemolysis); hypertonic — water leaves cells, cells shrink; given slowly under close watch.
7. Nurse's role: give only prescribed fluid at prescribed rate, maintain intake–output chart, watch for fluid overload (breathlessness, oedema) and electrolyte imbalance.
questions.question: Describe the various mechanisms of transport across the cell membrane. Add a note on the nursing significance of the tonicity of intravenous fluids.

questions.answer:
1. Total body water ≈ 60% of body weight in adult men (≈ 42 L in 70 kg); 50–55% in women; ≈ 75% in newborn; less in elderly.
2. Compartments: ICF two-thirds (40% of weight, ≈ 28 L); ECF one-third (20%, ≈ 14 L) = interstitial fluid ≈ 3/4 (10.5 L) + plasma ≈ 1/4 (3.5 L) + small transcellular fluid (CSF, synovial, pleural, aqueous, GI secretions).
3. Electrolytes: ECF rich in Na+ (135–145 mmol/L), Cl− (98–106), HCO3− (22–28); ICF rich in K+ (≈ 140), phosphate, proteins, Mg2+.
4. Functions: osmotic balance (Na+ decides ECF volume), nerve and muscle excitability, acid–base buffering, enzyme action, clotting (Ca2+).
5. Water intake: drinking (thirst centre in hypothalamus), food, metabolic water (~300 mL/day).
6. Water output: urine (main regulated route), insensible loss from skin and lungs (~700–900 mL), sweat, faeces (~100–200 mL).
7. Hormonal control: ADH (water reabsorption), aldosterone (Na+ retention, K+ loss), renin–angiotensin system, ANP (Na+ and water loss).
8. Between compartments: osmosis across cell membranes; Starling forces (capillary hydrostatic vs plasma oncotic pressure) between plasma and interstitial fluid; lymph returns excess.
9. Homeostasis by negative feedback, e.g. dehydration → ↑ osmolality → ADH + thirst → water retained and taken in.
10. Nursing: intake–output chart, daily weight, signs of dehydration and oedema, electrolyte monitoring.
questions.question: Describe the body fluid compartments and the distribution of total body water. Explain how water and electrolyte balance is maintained.

questions.answer:
1. Homeostasis: maintenance of a nearly constant internal environment (ECF) despite external change — temperature, glucose, pH, BP, water.
2. Components: receptor → control centre → effector.
3. Negative feedback: response opposes the change — rise in blood glucose → insulin → glucose falls; fall in BP → baroreceptor reflex → BP rises; rise in temperature → sweating.
4. Positive feedback: response increases the change until an event ends it — oxytocin in labour, blood clotting, LH surge before ovulation.
5. Most body control is negative feedback; failure of homeostasis = disease.
questions.question: Explain homeostasis with examples of negative and positive feedback.

questions.answer:
1. Na+–K+ ATPase is a membrane protein that carries out primary active transport.
2. For each ATP split it pumps 3 Na+ out of the cell and 2 K+ into it, against their gradients.
3. Keeps Na+ high in ECF and K+ high in ICF.
4. Functions: maintains resting membrane potential (inside negative); controls cell volume (prevents swelling); its Na+ gradient drives secondary active transport (glucose, amino acids) and Na+–H+ exchange; restores ion distribution after action potentials.
5. Uses a large share of the body's resting energy; inhibited when ATP falls (hypoxia) → cells swell.
questions.question: Write a short note on the sodium–potassium pump.

questions.answer:
1. Cell cycle: sequence of events by which a cell grows and divides into two.
2. Interphase: G1 — growth, normal work, checkpoint; S — DNA replicated; G2 — preparation and DNA check.
3. M phase (mitosis): prophase (chromosomes condense, spindle forms, nuclear membrane breaks), metaphase (chromosomes at equator), anaphase (chromatids separate to poles), telophase (nuclei re-form), followed by cytokinesis.
4. G0 — resting state outside the cycle (neurons, cardiac muscle).
5. Checkpoints prevent division of damaged cells; failure → cancer; anticancer drugs affect rapidly dividing cells (hair, gut, marrow).
questions.question: Describe the phases of the cell cycle.

questions.answer:
1. Haemostasis (minutes): vessel spasm, platelet plug, clot.
2. Inflammation (1–4 days): vasodilation, leakage, neutrophils then macrophages clear debris; redness, heat, swelling, pain.
3. Proliferation (day 3 to ~3 weeks): fibroblasts make collagen, new capillaries (granulation tissue), epithelium covers, wound contracts.
4. Maturation/remodelling (weeks to a year): collagen reorganised and strengthened, scar pales.
5. First intention (clean, edges together) vs second intention (gaping/infected, granulation from base).
6. Delaying factors: infection, poor blood supply, diabetes, malnutrition (protein, vitamin C, zinc), anaemia, old age, steroids, smoking, tension on wound.
questions.question: Describe the phases of wound healing and the factors that affect it.

questions.answer:
1. Mucous membrane — lines tracts open to the exterior (digestive, respiratory, urinary, reproductive); secretes mucus, protects, lubricates, traps microbes, absorbs in gut.
2. Serous membrane — parietal and visceral layers (pleura, pericardium, peritoneum); serous fluid reduces friction.
3. Synovial membrane — lines joint cavities, bursae; synovial fluid lubricates and nourishes cartilage.
4. Cutaneous membrane — skin; protection, temperature control.
5. Glands: exocrine (ducts — sweat, salivary, gastric), endocrine (hormones into blood — thyroid, pituitary), mixed (pancreas, gonads).
6. Modes of secretion: merocrine (salivary), apocrine (axillary sweat, mammary), holocrine (sebaceous).
questions.question: Write the types and functions of membranes and glands in the body.

questions.answer: Osmosis is the movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane from a solution of lower solute concentration to one of higher solute concentration. The pressure needed to stop it is the osmotic pressure.
questions.question: Define osmosis.

questions.answer: About 60% of body weight: intracellular fluid about 40% and extracellular fluid about 20% (interstitial about 15%, plasma about 5%).
questions.question: What percentage of body weight is total body water in an adult man, and how is it divided?

questions.answer: A solution with the same effective osmotic pressure as plasma, so red cells neither swell nor shrink in it. Example: 0.9% sodium chloride (normal saline).
questions.question: What is an isotonic solution? Give one example.

questions.answer:
1. O2 transport: about 97–98% bound to haemoglobin as oxyhaemoglobin; 2–3% dissolved in plasma. 1 g Hb binds about 1.34 mL O2; arterial blood about 97% saturated (SpO2 95–100%), venous about 75%.
2. Loading in lungs (PO2 104 mmHg) and unloading in tissues (PO2 40 mmHg or less).
3. Dissociation curve: % saturation vs PO2; S-shaped (sigmoid). Flat upper part keeps blood saturated even if PO2 falls; steep part releases much O2 for a small fall in tissue PO2. P50 ≈ 26–27 mmHg.
4. Shift to right (O2 released more easily): ↑PCO2, ↑H+, ↑temperature, ↑2,3-BPG — Bohr effect; occurs in active tissues.
5. Shift to left: opposite changes, fetal Hb, carbon monoxide (binds ~200× more strongly).
6. CO2 transport: as bicarbonate ~70%; carbamino compounds with Hb and proteins ~20–23%; dissolved ~7%.
7. In RBC: CO2 + H2O → H2CO3 (carbonic anhydrase) → H+ + HCO3−; H+ buffered by Hb; HCO3− moves to plasma in exchange for Cl− (chloride shift); reversed in lungs.
8. Haldane effect: deoxygenated Hb carries more CO2; oxygenation in lungs releases CO2.
9. Diagram of the curve and of the chloride shift.
10. Nursing: pulse oximetry, recognising hypoxia, oxygen therapy as prescribed, CO poisoning.
questions.question: Describe the transport of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the blood. Add a note on the oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve.

questions.answer:
1. Respiratory centres: medulla — dorsal respiratory group (basic rhythm, inspiratory) and ventral group (forced breathing); pons — pneumotaxic centre (limits inspiration, sets rate) and apneustic centre (prolongs inspiration).
2. Chemical control: central chemoreceptors in medulla respond to H+ in CSF formed from CO2 — rising PCO2 is the strongest drive; peripheral chemoreceptors — carotid bodies (IX) and aortic bodies (X) respond mainly to low PO2 (< 60 mmHg), also to CO2 and H+.
3. Reflex control: Hering–Breuer inflation reflex via vagus; irritant receptors (cough, sneeze); J receptors; proprioceptors in exercise.
4. Higher control: voluntary (speech, breath-holding), emotions, pain, temperature.
5. Hypoxia = O2 lack at tissue level. Types: hypoxic (low arterial PO2 — altitude, airway obstruction, pneumonia), anaemic (low Hb, CO poisoning), stagnant (slow flow — heart failure, shock), histotoxic (cells cannot use O2 — cyanide). Signs: restlessness, confusion, tachycardia, tachypnoea, later drowsiness, cyanosis, arrhythmia.
6. Cyanosis: bluish colour when reduced Hb in capillaries exceeds about 5 g/dL. Central (lips, tongue — lung disease, shunts) vs peripheral (nail beds, cold, low flow). Absent in severe anaemia and CO poisoning; marked in polycythaemia.
7. Nursing: count respiration for a full minute, positioning, SpO2 monitoring, oxygen as prescribed with care in CO2-retaining patients, airway care.
questions.question: Explain the regulation of respiration. Describe hypoxia and cyanosis.

questions.answer:
1. Air flows from high to low pressure; volume change alters pressure (Boyle's law).
2. Inspiration (active): diaphragm contracts and descends (≈ 75% of quiet breathing); external intercostals raise ribs and sternum (pump- and bucket-handle); thoracic volume ↑ → intrapleural pressure more negative (−2.5 to −6 mmHg) → lungs expand → alveolar pressure ≈ −1 mmHg → air enters.
3. Accessory muscles in deep breathing: sternocleidomastoid, scalenes, pectoralis minor.
4. Expiration (passive): muscles relax; elastic recoil and surface tension reduce volume → alveolar pressure ≈ +1 mmHg → air leaves.
5. Forced expiration: internal intercostals and abdominal muscles.
questions.question: Describe the mechanism of normal inspiration and expiration.

questions.answer:
1. Tidal volume — 500 mL (one quiet breath).
2. Inspiratory reserve volume — 3000 mL.
3. Expiratory reserve volume — 1100 mL.
4. Residual volume — 1200 mL (left after maximal expiration).
5. Inspiratory capacity (TV + IRV) — 3500 mL.
6. Functional residual capacity (ERV + RV) — 2300 mL.
7. Vital capacity (IRV + TV + ERV) — 4600 mL.
8. Total lung capacity (VC + RV) — 5800 mL.
9. Minute ventilation = TV × rate ≈ 6 L/min; dead space 150 mL; alveolar ventilation ≈ 4.2 L/min. Women about 20–25% lower.
questions.question: Define lung volumes and capacities with their normal values.

questions.answer:
1. Lipoprotein (mainly dipalmitoyl lecithin) secreted by type II alveolar cells.
2. Lowers surface tension of the fluid lining alveoli.
3. Prevents collapse of small alveoli at end of expiration; makes lungs easier to inflate (raises compliance); helps keep alveoli dry.
4. Formed mainly late in fetal life; deficiency in premature babies → respiratory distress syndrome (grunting, retractions, cyanosis).
5. Nursing: watch preterm babies closely; deep breathing after surgery keeps alveoli open.
questions.question: Write a note on surfactant and its importance.

questions.answer:
1. Receives the whole right ventricular output.
2. Low pressure (≈ 25/8 mmHg) and low resistance; short, thin, distensible vessels.
3. Hypoxic vasoconstriction diverts blood to well-ventilated alveoli (opposite of systemic vessels).
4. Low capillary pressure (≈ 7–10 mmHg) keeps alveoli dry; raised left atrial pressure → pulmonary oedema.
5. Acts as blood reservoir (~450–500 mL) and filter for small clots and air bubbles.
6. Gravity gives more flow to bases when standing.
7. Converts angiotensin I to II (ACE).
questions.question: Describe the functional features of the pulmonary circulation.

questions.answer:
1. Ventilation rises abruptly at the start (signals from motor cortex and joint proprioceptors), then steadily with rising CO2, H+ and temperature.
2. Tidal volume and rate both increase; minute ventilation can rise from ~6 L/min to 100 L/min or more.
3. O2 consumption rises; more O2 extracted in muscles due to right shift of dissociation curve.
4. Pulmonary blood flow and diffusing capacity increase as more capillaries open.
5. After exercise breathing stays raised to repay the oxygen debt (remove lactate, restore ATP and creatine phosphate).
6. Training improves efficiency.
questions.question: Explain the respiratory changes during exercise.

questions.answer: Bluish discolouration of skin and mucous membranes that appears when reduced (deoxygenated) haemoglobin in capillary blood exceeds about 5 g/dL.
questions.question: Define cyanosis.

questions.answer: Periodic breathing in which breaths gradually increase then decrease in depth, followed by a period of apnoea, in repeating cycles; seen in severe heart failure, brain damage and near death.
questions.question: What is Cheyne–Stokes breathing?

questions.answer: When CO2 enters red cells in the tissues, bicarbonate formed by carbonic anhydrase moves out into plasma and chloride ions move into the cell to keep electrical balance; it reverses in the lungs (Hamburger phenomenon).
questions.question: What is the chloride shift?

questions.answer:
1. Volume 1.5–2 L/day; pH 1–3.5.
2. Composition and functions: HCl (parietal cells) — kills microbes, activates pepsinogen, acid medium, helps iron and calcium absorption; intrinsic factor (parietal) — B12 absorption; pepsinogen (chief cells) → pepsin — protein digestion; gastric lipase; mucus and bicarbonate — protective barrier; gastrin (G cells) — stimulates acid and motility.
3. Mechanism of HCl secretion: CO2 + H2O → H2CO3 (carbonic anhydrase) → H+ + HCO3−; H+ pumped into lumen by H+–K+ ATPase; Cl− follows through channels; HCO3− exchanged for Cl− into blood → alkaline tide. Stimulants: acetylcholine, gastrin, histamine.
4. Regulation: cephalic phase (~30%) — sight, smell, thought of food via vagus; gastric phase (~60%) — distension and protein in stomach → local/vagal reflexes and gastrin; intestinal phase (~10%) — slight stimulation then mainly inhibition.
5. Inhibition: acid in antrum (pH < 2) stops gastrin; enterogastric reflex; secretin, CCK, GIP, somatostatin when acid, fat, hypertonic chyme reach duodenum.
6. Flow chart of phases.
7. Nursing: vomiting → loss of HCl → metabolic alkalosis; gastrectomy → B12 deficiency; stress and NSAIDs → ulcers; aspirate test for NG tube placement as per protocol.
questions.question: Describe the composition and functions of gastric juice. Explain the mechanism and regulation of gastric secretion.

questions.answer:
1. Carbohydrates: mouth — salivary amylase: starch → maltose, dextrins; stomach — amylase acts inside bolus until acid stops it; small intestine — pancreatic amylase → disaccharides; brush-border maltase, sucrase, lactase → glucose, fructose, galactose.
2. Absorption: glucose and galactose by Na+ cotransport (SGLT1) — secondary active; fructose by facilitated diffusion (GLUT5); into portal blood.
3. Proteins: stomach — pepsin → proteoses, peptones; small intestine — trypsin (activated by enterokinase), chymotrypsin, carboxypeptidase → small peptides; brush-border peptidases → amino acids, di- and tripeptides; absorbed by Na+/H+-coupled transport into portal blood.
4. Fats: small amounts by lingual and gastric lipase; bile salts emulsify; pancreatic lipase + colipase → monoglycerides + fatty acids; micelles carry them to the cell; re-formed into triglycerides, packed as chylomicrons → lacteals → thoracic duct; short-chain fatty acids directly to blood; fat-soluble vitamins with fats.
5. Adaptations: folds, villi, microvilli, lacteals, rich blood supply.
6. Water and minerals: water by osmosis; iron and calcium in duodenum; B12 with intrinsic factor in terminal ileum; bile salts reabsorbed in ileum.
7. Table summarising enzymes, substrates and products.
8. Nursing: ORS uses glucose–sodium cotransport; fat malabsorption in obstructive jaundice; lactose intolerance; enteral feeding.
questions.question: Describe the digestion and absorption of carbohydrates, proteins and fats.

questions.answer:
1. 1–1.5 L/day, pH 6–7.4; 99.5% water; amylase (ptyalin), lingual lipase, mucin, lysozyme, IgA, electrolytes.
2. Regulation purely nervous: parasympathetic via facial (submandibular, sublingual) and glossopharyngeal (parotid) → copious watery saliva; sympathetic → scanty thick saliva; unconditioned and conditioned reflexes.
3. Functions: lubrication and bolus formation, starch digestion, taste, cleansing and protection of mouth and teeth, buffering, speech, thirst signal, excretion of some substances.
questions.question: Write the composition, regulation and functions of saliva.

questions.answer:
1. 1.2–1.5 L/day; pH ≈ 8; rich in bicarbonate.
2. Enzymes: trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, procarboxypeptidase (activated via enterokinase → trypsin), amylase, lipase with colipase, phospholipase, cholesterol esterase, nucleases.
3. Functions: neutralises acid chyme; digests proteins, carbohydrates, fats, nucleic acids.
4. Regulation: vagus (cephalic/gastric) — enzymes; secretin (acid in duodenum) — bicarbonate-rich watery juice; CCK (fat, protein in duodenum) — enzyme-rich juice.
5. Premature activation of trypsin → acute pancreatitis.
questions.question: Describe the composition, functions and regulation of pancreatic juice.

questions.answer:
1. 500–1000 mL/day from liver; stored and concentrated 5–10× in gall bladder.
2. Composition: water, bile salts (glycocholate, taurocholate), bile pigments (bilirubin), cholesterol, lecithin, electrolytes, bicarbonate.
3. Functions: emulsification of fat; micelle formation for absorption of fats and vitamins A, D, E, K; excretion of bilirubin, cholesterol, drugs; neutralises acid; mild laxative.
4. Enterohepatic circulation: 90–95% bile salts reabsorbed in terminal ileum.
5. Gall bladder contracts under CCK.
6. Obstruction → steatorrhoea, vitamin K deficiency, obstructive jaundice.
questions.question: Write the composition and functions of bile.

questions.answer:
1. Carbohydrate metabolism — glycogenesis, glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis.
2. Fat metabolism — lipoproteins, cholesterol, ketone bodies.
3. Protein metabolism — deamination, urea formation, plasma proteins (albumin, fibrinogen, prothrombin, clotting factors).
4. Bile formation and excretion of bilirubin.
5. Storage — glycogen, vitamins A, D, B12, iron, copper.
6. Detoxification and drug metabolism; breakdown of hormones.
7. Kupffer cells — defence.
8. Heat production; fetal haemopoiesis; activation of vitamin D (first step).
questions.question: List the functions of the liver.

questions.answer:
1. Small intestine: segmentation (mixing, contact with mucosa); peristalsis (propulsion); migrating motor complex between meals.
2. Large intestine: haustral churning (slow mixing, water absorption); mass movements 2–3 times a day, often after meals (gastrocolic reflex).
3. Defaecation reflex: faeces stretch rectum → afferents to sacral cord S2–S4 → parasympathetic contraction of rectum and relaxation of internal sphincter; external sphincter voluntary (pudendal nerve); straining raises abdominal pressure.
4. Nursing: fibre, fluids, activity, regular time after meals to prevent constipation.
questions.question: Describe the movements of the small and large intestine and the defaecation reflex.

questions.answer: A glycoprotein secreted by parietal cells of the stomach that binds vitamin B12 and allows its absorption in the terminal ileum. Deficiency causes B12 deficiency — pernicious (megaloblastic) anaemia.
questions.question: What is intrinsic factor? What happens in its deficiency?

questions.answer: Secretin — watery, bicarbonate-rich juice; cholecystokinin (CCK) — enzyme-rich juice and gall bladder contraction.
questions.question: Name the hormones that stimulate pancreatic secretion and state their effects.

questions.answer: Recycling of bile salts: about 90–95% are reabsorbed in the terminal ileum, carried back to the liver in portal blood and secreted again in bile.
questions.question: What is enterohepatic circulation?

questions.answer:
1. Definition: lateral pressure exerted by blood on the walls of arteries; normal ≈ 120/80 mmHg; pulse pressure ≈ 40; MAP = DP + 1/3 PP ≈ 93 mmHg. BP = cardiac output × peripheral resistance.
2. Factors: cardiac output (heart rate, stroke volume), peripheral resistance (arteriolar diameter), blood volume, viscosity, elasticity of arteries, age, sex, posture, exercise, emotion, sleep, meals, body build.
3. Short-term nervous regulation: baroreceptor reflex — carotid sinus (IX) and aortic arch (X); ↑BP → ↑vagal, ↓sympathetic → ↓HR, vasodilation → BP falls; reverse for low BP. Chemoreceptor reflex; CNS ischaemic response (Cushing's reflex).
4. Hormonal: renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (angiotensin II vasoconstriction, aldosterone salt retention, ADH, thirst); ADH; adrenaline and noradrenaline; ANP (lowers BP).
5. Long-term renal control: pressure natriuresis — kidneys adjust salt and water excretion and blood volume.
6. Capillary fluid shift.
7. Flow chart of the baroreceptor reflex.
8. Hypertension ≥ 140/90 on repeated readings; hypotension; postural hypotension.
9. Nursing: correct BP technique (cuff size, rest 5 min, arm at heart level), lying and standing readings, dangling before standing, report changes.
questions.question: Define blood pressure. Describe the factors influencing blood pressure and explain its regulation.

questions.answer:
1. Haemostasis: vascular spasm → platelet plug → coagulation → clot retraction → fibrinolysis.
2. Platelet plug: adhesion to collagen via von Willebrand factor; activation and release of ADP, thromboxane A2, serotonin; aggregation.
3. Clotting factors I–XIII (no VI); mostly made in liver.
4. Intrinsic pathway: contact with collagen → XII → XI → IX (+VIII, Ca2+, platelet phospholipid) → activates X.
5. Extrinsic pathway: tissue factor (III) + VII → activates X (faster).
6. Common pathway: Xa + Va + Ca2+ + phospholipid = prothrombin activator → prothrombin (II) → thrombin → fibrinogen (I) → fibrin; XIII cross-links fibrin → stable clot; thrombin's positive feedback.
7. Clot retraction (platelets) and fibrinolysis (plasminogen → plasmin by tPA).
8. Diagram of the cascade.
9. Tests: bleeding time 1–5 min (platelets, vessels); clotting time 4–10 min; PT ~11–16 s (extrinsic, INR); aPTT ~25–40 s (intrinsic) — lab values vary.
10. Vitamin K needed for II, VII, IX, X; deficiency in newborns, obstructive jaundice, prolonged antibiotics → bleeding; warfarin-type drugs act against it.
11. Nursing: bleeding precautions, pressure after venepuncture, watch for petechiae, haemophilia (VIII, IX).
questions.question: Describe the mechanism of blood coagulation. Add a note on bleeding time, clotting time and the role of vitamin K.

questions.answer:
1. Events of one heartbeat; 0.8 s at 75/min: atrial systole 0.1, ventricular systole 0.3, ventricular diastole 0.5 s.
2. Atrial systole tops up ventricles.
3. Isovolumetric contraction — AV valves close (S1); all valves closed.
4. Ejection — semilunar valves open.
5. Isovolumetric relaxation — semilunar valves close (S2).
6. Rapid filling — AV valves open; slow filling (diastasis).
7. Tachycardia shortens diastole more than systole → less filling and coronary flow.
questions.question: Describe the cardiac cycle.

questions.answer:
1. Specialised muscle that starts and spreads impulses.
2. SA node (right atrium near SVC) — pacemaker, 70–80/min.
3. Impulse spreads over atria → AV node — delay ~0.1 s so atria empty first.
4. Bundle of His → right and left bundle branches → Purkinje fibres → ventricles from apex upward.
5. Intrinsic rates: AV node 40–60, Purkinje 15–40/min (take over if SA fails).
6. ECG: P (atrial depolarisation), QRS (ventricular depolarisation), T (ventricular repolarisation).
7. Vagus slows, sympathetic speeds.
questions.question: Explain the conduction system of the heart.

questions.answer:
1. Cardiac output = volume pumped by each ventricle per minute = stroke volume × heart rate ≈ 70 × 72 ≈ 5 L/min; cardiac index ≈ 3.2 L/min/m².
2. Preload/venous return — Frank–Starling law: greater stretch → stronger contraction.
3. Contractility — ↑ by sympathetic, adrenaline, thyroxine, calcium; ↓ by hypoxia, acidosis, damage.
4. Afterload — high BP, aortic stenosis reduce SV.
5. Heart rate — ↑ output up to a limit; very fast rates reduce filling.
6. Physiological variations: exercise, posture, emotion, pregnancy, age.
questions.question: Define cardiac output. What are the factors affecting it?

questions.answer:
1. Formation of RBCs in red marrow (adult: flat bones, vertebrae, ends of long bones).
2. Stages: stem cell → proerythroblast → early, intermediate, late normoblast (nucleus lost) → reticulocyte → RBC (~7 days).
3. Factors: erythropoietin from kidney (in hypoxia); iron; vitamin B12 and folic acid (DNA synthesis); intrinsic factor; proteins; vitamin C, copper, cobalt, B6; thyroxine, androgens.
4. Deficiencies: iron → microcytic anaemia; B12/folate → megaloblastic anaemia; kidney failure → anaemia.
5. RBC life 120 days; destroyed in spleen.
questions.question: Describe the stages and factors of erythropoiesis.

questions.answer:
1. ABO depends on A and B antigens on RBCs; plasma has antibodies against absent antigens.
2. A — anti-B; B — anti-A; AB — no antibodies (universal recipient); O — anti-A and anti-B (universal donor of red cells).
3. Rh: D antigen present = Rh+; anti-D forms only after exposure.
4. Haemolytic disease of the newborn: Rh− mother sensitised by Rh+ fetus; later pregnancy antibodies destroy fetal RBCs; prevented by anti-D immunoglobulin as per protocol.
5. Importance: transfusion (grouping and cross-matching), pregnancy, transplants; mismatched transfusion → haemolysis, fever, back pain, shock, renal failure.
questions.question: Write a note on the ABO and Rh blood group systems.

questions.answer: About 120 days; old red cells are destroyed mainly in the spleen (also liver and marrow) by macrophages of the reticuloendothelial system.
questions.question: State the normal life span of red blood cells and where they are destroyed.

questions.answer: Factors II (prothrombin), VII, IX and X (also proteins C and S).
questions.question: Name the vitamin K-dependent clotting factors.

questions.answer: The difference between the apical heart rate and the radial pulse rate counted at the same time; seen in atrial fibrillation when some beats are too weak to reach the wrist.
questions.question: What is pulse deficit?

questions.answer:
1. Pituitary controlled by hypothalamus: anterior lobe via releasing hormones in hypophyseal portal veins; posterior lobe via nerve fibres.
2. Growth hormone: growth of bone and muscle, protein synthesis, fat breakdown, raises blood glucose; excess → gigantism (child), acromegaly (adult); deficiency → dwarfism.
3. TSH — thyroid growth and T3/T4 secretion.
4. ACTH — cortisol secretion.
5. FSH — follicle growth and oestrogen; spermatogenesis.
6. LH — ovulation, corpus luteum; testosterone.
7. Prolactin — milk production.
8. Posterior pituitary (made in hypothalamus): ADH — water reabsorption in collecting ducts; lack → diabetes insipidus (polyuria, thirst); excess → SIADH (low sodium). Oxytocin — uterine contraction in labour, milk ejection.
9. Feedback control diagram.
10. Nursing: intake–output and urine specific gravity in DI; growth monitoring in children; oxytocin effects in labour.
questions.question: Describe the hormones of the pituitary gland, their functions and disorders.

questions.answer:
1. Cortex — zona glomerulosa: aldosterone — Na+ and water retention, K+ and H+ excretion, maintains BP; controlled by angiotensin II and K+.
2. Zona fasciculata: cortisol — gluconeogenesis, raises blood glucose; protein breakdown, fat mobilisation; anti-inflammatory, immunosuppressive; stress response; needed for vascular response; controlled by ACTH; diurnal (morning peak).
3. Zona reticularis: androgens — pubic and axillary hair.
4. Medulla: adrenaline and noradrenaline under sympathetic stimulation — fight or flight: ↑ HR and BP, bronchodilation, pupil dilation, glycogenolysis, blood to muscles.
5. Disorders: Cushing's syndrome (moon face, buffalo hump, striae, high sugar and BP); Addison's disease (weakness, low BP, low Na+, high K+, pigmentation); Conn's syndrome (hypertension, low K+); phaeochromocytoma (episodic hypertension, sweating, palpitations).
6. Nursing: do not stop long-term steroids suddenly; monitor glucose, BP, infection; fluid and electrolyte watch.
questions.question: Describe the hormones of the adrenal gland and their functions. Mention the disorders.

questions.answer:
1. Increase BMR, O2 consumption and heat production.
2. Essential for growth and brain development (lack in infancy → cretinism).
3. Carbohydrate absorption and use ↑; fat breakdown ↑, cholesterol ↓; protein synthesis.
4. Heart rate and output ↑.
5. Alertness, reflexes.

# Unit 1: General physiology — cell, body fluids, tissues, membranes and glands

This unit covers INC Unit I (4 hours). Anatomy tells you what the cell and tissues look like; physiology tells you how they work. Almost every nursing action that involves fluids, electrolytes, wounds or infusions rests on the ideas in this unit.

## 1.1 Physiology and homeostasis

**Physiology** is the study of the normal functions of the living body and its parts.

**Homeostasis** is the maintenance of a nearly constant internal environment (the extracellular fluid) in spite of changes outside the body. Body temperature, blood glucose, blood pH, blood pressure, plasma sodium and water content are all kept within narrow limits.

Every homeostatic system has three parts:

| Part | Job | Example: body temperature |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Receptor (sensor) | Detects a change | Thermoreceptors in skin and hypothalamus |
| Control centre | Compares with the set point and decides | Hypothalamus |
| Effector | Carries out the correction | Sweat glands, skin blood vessels, skeletal muscle (shivering) |

### Negative and positive feedback

- **Negative feedback** — the response *opposes* the original change and brings the value back to normal. Most body control works this way. Examples: a rise in blood glucose → insulin → glucose falls; a fall in blood pressure → baroreceptor reflex → heart rate and vessel tone rise.
- **Positive feedback** — the response *increases* the original change until some event ends it. It is used only for short, self-limiting events. Examples: oxytocin and uterine contractions during labour; clotting of blood; the rise of sodium entry during the upstroke of a nerve action potential; the LH surge before ovulation.

```text
Negative feedback loop

  Change (e.g. BP falls)
        │
        ▼
  Receptor (baroreceptors) ──► Control centre (medulla)
                                      │
                                      ▼
                              Effector (heart, arterioles)
                                      │
                                      ▼
                     Response opposes the change (BP rises back)
```

## 1.2 Cell physiology

The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of the body. Its main parts and their work:

| Part | Main function |
| --- | --- |
| Cell (plasma) membrane | Boundary; controls what enters and leaves; carries receptors |
| Nucleus | Holds DNA; controls protein synthesis and cell division |
| Mitochondria | Aerobic respiration; make most of the cell's ATP ("power house") |
| Ribosomes | Protein synthesis |
| Rough endoplasmic reticulum | Makes proteins for export and for membranes |
| Smooth endoplasmic reticulum | Lipid and steroid synthesis, detoxification, calcium store in muscle |
| Golgi apparatus | Packs, modifies and dispatches proteins in vesicles |
| Lysosomes | Digestive enzymes; break down worn-out parts and engulfed bacteria |
| Peroxisomes | Break down fatty acids and hydrogen peroxide |
| Cytoskeleton, centrosome | Shape, movement, spindle formation during division |

### The cell membrane

The membrane is a **lipid bilayer** (phospholipids with water-loving heads outward and water-fearing tails inward) with proteins floating in it — the **fluid mosaic model**. Cholesterol keeps it stable; carbohydrate chains on the outer surface act as identity markers (for example blood group antigens).

Membrane proteins act as channels, carriers, pumps, receptors for hormones and enzymes. Because the core is fatty, lipid-soluble substances (O2, CO2, alcohol, steroid hormones) pass easily, while ions and glucose need proteins to cross.

## 1.3 Transport across the cell membrane

```text
Transport across membrane
├── Passive (no ATP; down the concentration gradient)
│     ├── Simple diffusion
│     ├── Facilitated diffusion (carrier or channel)
│     ├── Osmosis (water)
│     └── Filtration (pushed by hydrostatic pressure)
├── Active (uses ATP; can go against the gradient)
│     ├── Primary active transport (Na+–K+ pump)
│     └── Secondary active transport (cotransport, countertransport)
└── Vesicular transport (bulk; uses ATP)
      ├── Endocytosis: phagocytosis, pinocytosis, receptor-mediated
      └── Exocytosis
```

### Passive transport

- **Simple diffusion** — molecules move from a region of higher concentration to lower concentration until evenly spread. Gas exchange in the lungs is the classic example. The rate rises with a larger concentration difference, larger surface area, higher temperature and thinner membrane, and falls with larger molecular size.
- **Facilitated diffusion** — still down the gradient, but a carrier protein helps. Glucose enters most cells this way (GLUT carriers). It shows *saturation*: once all carriers are busy, the rate cannot rise further.
- **Osmosis** — movement of **water** across a selectively permeable membrane from a dilute solution (more water) to a concentrated solution (less water). The pressure needed to stop it is the **osmotic pressure**. Plasma osmolality is about 285–295 mOsm/kg water.
- **Filtration** — water and small solutes are pushed through a membrane by hydrostatic pressure, for example at the glomerulus and at the arterial end of capillaries.

### Tonicity — why it matters at the bedside

| Solution | Effect on red cells | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Isotonic | No change in size | 0.9% sodium chloride (normal saline), 5% glucose at first |
| Hypotonic | Water enters; cells swell and may burst (haemolysis) | Plain water, 0.45% saline |
| Hypertonic | Water leaves; cells shrink (crenation) | 3% saline, 10% glucose |

### Active transport

- **Primary active transport** uses ATP directly. The **sodium–potassium pump (Na+–K+ ATPase)** pushes **3 Na+ out** and takes **2 K+ in** for each ATP. It keeps Na+ high outside and K+ high inside, helps maintain the resting membrane potential and controls cell volume. Other pumps: calcium pump, the H+–K+ pump of gastric parietal cells.
- **Secondary active transport** uses the Na+ gradient made by the pump. In **cotransport (symport)** Na+ and another substance move in the same direction (Na+–glucose in the gut and kidney tubules). In **countertransport (antiport)** they move in opposite directions (Na+–H+ exchange in kidney tubules).

### Vesicular (bulk) transport

- **Endocytosis** — the membrane folds around material and pinches off a vesicle. **Phagocytosis** ("cell eating") is taking in large particles such as bacteria by neutrophils and macrophages. **Pinocytosis** ("cell drinking") takes in droplets of fluid. **Receptor-mediated endocytosis** takes up specific substances such as LDL cholesterol.
- **Exocytosis** — vesicles fuse with the membrane and release contents outside: hormones, neurotransmitters, digestive enzymes, mucus.

## 1.4 Body fluid compartments

Water is the largest single component of the body. In a young adult man it is about **60% of body weight**; in women about 50–55% (more fat, which holds little water); in a newborn about 75%; in the elderly it falls to about 45–50%.

```text
Total body water (about 60% of body weight; 42 L in a 70 kg man)
├── Intracellular fluid (ICF) — 2/3 — about 40% of body weight (≈ 28 L)
└── Extracellular fluid (ECF) — 1/3 — about 20% of body weight (≈ 14 L)
      ├── Interstitial fluid (incl. lymph) — about 3/4 of ECF (≈ 10.5 L)
      ├── Plasma — about 1/4 of ECF (≈ 3.5 L)
      └── Transcellular fluid — small: CSF, synovial, pleural, aqueous humour, GI secretions
```

### Major electrolytes

| Ion | ECF (plasma) | ICF |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sodium (Na+) | High: about 135–145 mmol/L — main ECF cation | Low (about 10–14) |
| Potassium (K+) | Low: about 3.5–5.0 mmol/L | High (about 140) — main ICF cation |
| Chloride (Cl−) | High: about 98–106 mmol/L — main ECF anion | Low |
| Bicarbonate (HCO3−) | About 22–28 mmol/L | Low |
| Phosphate, proteins | Low | High — main ICF anions |
| Magnesium (Mg2+) | Low | Relatively high |
| Calcium (Ca2+) | About 9–10.5 mg/dL total in plasma | Very low in cytosol |

Laboratory reference ranges differ slightly; always read the range printed on the report.

**Functions of electrolytes**: control of osmotic pressure and water distribution (Na+ decides ECF volume); nerve and muscle excitability (Na+, K+, Ca2+); acid–base buffering (HCO3−, phosphate, proteins); enzyme activity; blood clotting (Ca2+); bone (Ca2+, phosphate).

### How water and electrolytes are kept in balance

- **Intake** — drinking (thirst centre in hypothalamus), food, and water made by metabolism (about 300 mL a day).
- **Output** — urine (largest and the only one finely controlled), insensible loss through skin and breath (about 700–900 mL a day in an adult at rest), sweat, faeces (about 100–200 mL).
- **Hormonal control** — ADH (water), aldosterone (sodium reabsorption, potassium excretion), atrial natriuretic peptide (sodium loss), the renin–angiotensin system.
- **Between compartments** — water moves freely across cell membranes by osmosis, so a fall in ECF sodium draws water into cells (cell swelling, brain oedema), and a rise draws water out (cell shrinkage). Between plasma and interstitial fluid, the balance of capillary hydrostatic pressure and plasma protein (oncotic) pressure decides fluid movement (Starling forces).

**Oedema** is excess fluid in the interstitial space. Causes: raised capillary pressure (heart failure, venous obstruction), low plasma proteins (malnutrition, liver disease, nephrotic syndrome), leaky capillaries (inflammation, burns), blocked lymphatics (filariasis), sodium retention.

## 1.5 The cell cycle

The cell cycle is the sequence of events by which a cell grows and divides into two daughter cells.

```text
     ┌──────────── Interphase (about 90% of the time) ────────────┐
     G1 (growth, normal work) ──► S (DNA copied) ──► G2 (prepare) ──► M (mitosis + cytokinesis)
      ▲                                                                       │
      └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
     G0 = resting phase: cell has left the cycle (e.g. neurons, most adult cardiac muscle)
```

- **G1 phase** — cell grows, makes proteins and organelles; checkpoint decides whether to divide.
- **S phase** — DNA is replicated, so each chromosome becomes two sister chromatids.
- **G2 phase** — final growth; checks that DNA is copied correctly.
- **M phase (mitosis)** — prophase (chromosomes condense, nuclear membrane breaks down, spindle forms), metaphase (chromosomes line up at the equator), anaphase (chromatids pulled to opposite poles), telophase (nuclear membranes re-form) — followed by **cytokinesis** (cytoplasm divides). Mitosis gives two identical diploid (46-chromosome) cells; it is used for growth and repair.
- **Meiosis** — two divisions that halve the chromosome number to 23 (haploid); it occurs only in the gonads to form ova and sperm and creates genetic variation (crossing over).

**Checkpoints** stop a cell with damaged DNA from dividing. When this control fails, cells divide without restraint — the basis of cancer. Many anticancer treatments and radiotherapy act on rapidly dividing cells, which is why hair follicles, gut lining and bone marrow are affected.

**Cells by ability to divide**: labile cells divide throughout life (skin, gut lining, bone marrow); stable cells divide when needed (liver, kidney tubules); permanent cells cannot divide (neurons, cardiac muscle) — damage heals by scar.

## 1.6 Tissues — formation and repair

**Tissue** = a group of similar cells with the intercellular material that together do one job. The four basic tissues are epithelial, connective, muscular and nervous. All tissues develop from the three germ layers of the embryo (ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm).

### Tissue repair

1. **Regeneration** — dead cells are replaced by the same kind of cells, so normal structure and function return. Possible in labile and stable cells when the supporting framework is intact (for example a skin graze, liver after partial damage).
2. **Repair by fibrosis (scar)** — when damage is large or the cells cannot divide, the gap is filled with granulation tissue that becomes fibrous scar. Function of that part is lost (scar after myocardial infarction).

### Phases of wound healing

| Phase | Approximate time | What happens |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Haemostasis | Minutes | Vessel spasm, platelet plug, clot seals the wound |
| Inflammation | First 1–4 days | Vessels dilate and leak; neutrophils then macrophages clear debris and bacteria; redness, warmth, swelling, pain |
| Proliferation | About day 3 to 3 weeks | Fibroblasts lay down collagen; new capillaries form (granulation tissue — red, granular); epithelium grows over; wound contracts |
| Maturation (remodelling) | 3 weeks to a year or more | Collagen reorganised and strengthened; scar pales and flattens |

- **Healing by first intention** — clean, closely joined edges (surgical incision); little granulation tissue, thin scar.
- **Healing by second intention** — gaping or infected wound; fills from the base with much granulation tissue; slow, large scar.

**Factors that delay healing**: poor blood supply, infection, foreign body, diabetes, malnutrition (low protein, vitamin C, zinc), anaemia, old age, corticosteroid therapy, smoking, movement or tension on the wound.

## 1.7 Membranes and glands — functions

### Membranes

| Membrane | Where | Function |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mucous membrane | Lines tracts open to the outside: digestive, respiratory, urinary, reproductive | Secretes mucus; protects, lubricates, traps dust and microbes; absorbs (gut) |
| Serous membrane | Two layers (parietal and visceral) lining closed cavities: pleura, pericardium, peritoneum | Secretes thin serous fluid so organs glide without friction |
| Synovial membrane | Lines cavities of freely movable joints, bursae, tendon sheaths | Secretes synovial fluid that lubricates and nourishes articular cartilage |
| Cutaneous membrane | The skin | Protection, temperature control, sensation |

### Glands

A **gland** is a cell or group of cells that makes and releases a secretion.

- **Exocrine glands** release secretions through **ducts** onto a surface or into a cavity: sweat, salivary, sebaceous, gastric glands, exocrine pancreas, liver (bile).
- **Endocrine glands** are ductless and release **hormones into the blood**: pituitary, thyroid, adrenals, islets of pancreas.
- **Mixed glands** do both: pancreas, testis, ovary.

By the way they release secretion:

| Type | How | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Merocrine (eccrine) | Secretion leaves by exocytosis; cell intact | Salivary, most sweat glands |
| Apocrine | Top part of the cell breaks off with the secretion | Axillary sweat glands, mammary (fat part) |
| Holocrine | Whole cell bursts and becomes the secretion | Sebaceous glands |

## 1.8 Application and implication in nursing

- **Intravenous fluids** — knowing tonicity explains why isotonic saline expands ECF, why too much hypotonic fluid can cause cell (including brain) swelling, and why hypertonic fluid is given slowly under close watch. Fluids, their type and rate are always as prescribed.
- **Intake–output chart** — the nurse measures all intake and output to judge fluid balance; daily weight under the same conditions is the best bedside guide to body water change.
- **Dehydration** — dry mouth, thirst, poor skin turgor, sunken eyes, low urine output, rising pulse; infants and the elderly dehydrate fastest because of their water proportions and weaker thirst.
- **Oedema** — assess pitting, elevate limbs, turn often (oedematous skin breaks down easily), restrict sodium or fluid when ordered.
- **Electrolyte watch** — low potassium causes muscle weakness and heart rhythm problems; vomiting and diarrhoea, diuretics and wound drainage all cause losses.
- **Wound care** — aseptic technique, adequate protein and vitamin C, control of blood sugar, pressure relief and early detection of infection all speed healing.
- **Cancer therapy** — patients on drugs that kill dividing cells need mouth care, infection prevention and monitoring of blood counts, because labile tissues are hit first.

## Remember

- Homeostasis keeps the ECF constant; most control is by negative feedback; positive feedback is rare (labour, clotting, LH surge).
- Passive transport needs no ATP (diffusion, facilitated diffusion, osmosis, filtration); the Na+–K+ pump moves 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in per ATP.
- Total body water ≈ 60% of body weight: ICF 40%, ECF 20% (interstitial 15%, plasma 5%).
- Na+ and Cl− are the main ECF ions; K+ and phosphate the main ICF ions.
- Cell cycle: G1 → S (DNA copy) → G2 → M; neurons and cardiac muscle sit in G0 and heal by scar.
- Wound healing: haemostasis → inflammation → proliferation → remodelling.
- Mucous membranes line open tracts, serous membranes line closed cavities, synovial membranes line joints.
- Exocrine glands have ducts; endocrine glands release hormones into blood; sebaceous glands are holocrine.
